messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Shopowner
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mele had owned the same small neighborhood shop for years, a narrow storefront where she knew regular customers by name and usually stayed through closing herself. She is a 66-year-old divorced woman of Oceanian background, practical and self-reliant in the way many people had always described her, and that image of herself mattered to her. The event that now dominates her life happened one evening at closing time, at the same hour when the light outside was fading and she was counting the till behind the counter. Police came into the shop during a tense encounter that escalated quickly. In her account, what remains strongest is not a smooth sequence but sharp, disconnected moments: uniforms filling the doorway, the sense that every movement of hers was being tracked, the hard brightness of being scrutinized, her body going light and unsteady. She remembers feeling dizzy, trying to orient herself, and then the scene becoming fragmented. There are parts she cannot recover no matter how hard she tries. When she attempts to describe it, she stops, shakes her head, and says it does not come out right; the whole thing feels too extreme, almost like something she watched happen to another person rather than to herself.

In the weeks afterward, the time of day when it happened began to take on a particular force. Late afternoon into early evening, especially as the shop approached closing, became difficult to bear. Around that hour she would notice her body first: a lightheaded, floating sensation, the same unsteady feeling she had during the incident. If a customer lingered in the doorway watching her, or if she caught sight of someone standing outside the front window, she would stiffen immediately. What frightened her was not only the sensation itself but what it seemed to say about her. She had come to believe that a stronger person would have put the event behind her, that someone competent would not unravel because of a glance or an hour on the clock. She was certain that these reactions meant there was something fundamentally inadequate about her. At times, when the dizziness came and her thoughts scattered, she feared she was going crazy.

Because the event happened as daylight drained from the street, darkness itself became something she worked hard not to be in. At first this looked like practical caution. She changed the shop’s hours, closing earlier so she would not have to remain inside as evening set in. She asked customers to finish quickly near closing and became uneasy if anyone browsed without buying, especially if they seemed merely to stand and look. Over months, this changed the rhythm of the business. Regulars noticed that Mele no longer kept the old hours, and some stopped coming by after work because she was already shut. She avoided any circumstance that felt too close to that evening: being alone in dim light, locking up at dusk, standing in the quiet shop when the day’s bustle had ended. Dates connected to the event also became days she tried not to mark. As they approached, she would keep herself busy, refuse invitations, and tell herself it was just another day, while carefully arranging not to be at the shop at the same time or under the same conditions.

At home, where there was no counter to wipe down and no customer to serve, she sometimes turned to impulsive spending. She would order things she did not need or buy household items in multiples, describing it less as pleasure than as a brief interruption, a way to give her mind somewhere else to go. Packages accumulated unopened. The spending embarrassed her afterward and fed the same harsh self-judgment: proof, in her mind, that she was a lousy coper.

When she speaks about the incident now, there is still a halting quality to it. She can circle around the event more easily than go through it. She knows what hour is coming before she looks at the clock. She notices where people are standing in relation to her, who seems to be looking, whether the room is getting darker, whether her body feels even slightly light. She is seeking help now because the shop, once the steadiest part of her life, no longer feels like her own place at closing time, and because she is tired of organizing her days around not feeling what she feels. What she fears most is that the dizziness, the gaps in memory, and the unreality of it all mean she is losing her mind. What she hopes, though she says this cautiously, is to be able to stay in her shop until evening again without feeling watched, without bracing for that hour as if it were happening all over.
